title: Teamtailor ships jobs as a JSON Feed — the data you want is nested one level down
author: Devil Scrapes
summary: Quick answer Teamtailor powers the career sites of thousands of European scale-ups, and unlike most ATS platforms it publishes each customer's open roles as a JSON Feed at https://{subdomain}.teamtailor.com/jobs.json — no key, no login, no browser. The catch is that the useful structured data isn't in the feed envelope at all: each feed item wraps a nested schema.org JobPosting object, and the fields you actually want (location, hiring organization, publication date) live one level down inside it. The Teamtailor Jobs Scraper flattens that nesting across as many company subdomains as you hand it, at $0.0015 per job row plus a $0.005 run-start charge — $1.505 for 1,000 postings . The feed envelope isn't the job — the nested JobPosting is 📦 A JSON Feed item gives you title , url , and content_html . That's a blog-post shape, because JSON Feed was designed for blogs. Teamtailor reuses it for jobs and puts the real hiring data in an embedded schema.org JobPosting payload attached to each item. So title at the item level and title inside the JobPosting are two different things that can disagree, and everything a recruiter or market analyst actually filters on — jobLocation.address.addressLocality , addressRegion , addressCountry , hiringOrganization.name , datePublished — exists only in the nested object. A scraper that reads the envelope and stops gets you a list of links and some HTML blobs. We read both levels and emit a flat row: location_locality , location_region , location_country , hiring_organization_name , and a resolved date_published that falls back to the item-level date when the JobPosting omits it. job_id arrives as a string that isn't always a number 🔢 Teamtailor's job identifiers come through as strings, and the obvious move — int(value) — throws the moment a subdomain sends something non-numeric. That's a per-item parse error, and in a naive implementation it takes down the whole run: you asked for 40 companies, one of them had one odd ID, and you got zero rows. We validate before coercing: the value has to be a digit string (leading - allowed) before it becomes an integer, and anything else resolves to null rather than raising. The row still ships with its title, URL, and location intact — a missing ID is a degraded row, not a dead run. This is the same rule we apply everywhere: one bad item skips itself, it never kills the batch. description_text is stripped HTML, and description_html is opt-in ✂️ Every posting's body arrives as content_html — recruiter-authored markup, which in practice means inconsistent tags, nested lists, inline styles, and a lot of   . If you're feeding a model, matching keywords, or loading a warehouse column, you want text. So description_text is always populated: tags stripped, whitespace collapsed to single spaces. The raw markup is available too, but only when you ask for it via includeHtml — because on a 1,000-row pull the HTML is usually the single largest thing in your dataset, and most pipelines throw it away. Defaulting it off keeps your storage and your token bills smaller. What we handle for you 🛡️ A public JSON endpoint is not the same thing as a stable one, and this is where a weekend script diverges from a product: Pagination is merged, not truncated. Feeds page; we walk them and merge items into one response per company, so a 400-role employer doesn't silently become a 20-role one. Rate limits are obeyed, not guessed. When the server sends a Retry-After header, we use that number instead of an invented backoff, and we rotate both the proxy session and the browser-impersonation profile between attempts. Per-company fault isolation. Hand us 50 subdomains and one has been renamed, offboarded, or is briefly 503-ing — that company is logged and skipped, and the other 49 still return rows. The cap is applied after parsing. maxJobsPerCompany truncates the parsed result set, so you get the first N valid rows rather than N attempts, some of which were duds. Who this is for Recruiting-intelligence and job-board teams aggregating live European tech roles — Teamtailor's customer base skews toward Nordic and EU scale-ups that don't appear in US-centric ATS feeds. Sales teams selling into hiring companies — an open role is a budget signal, and hiring_organization_name plus posting velocity per subdomain is a cleaner buying trigger than firmographics. Labour-market researchers who need typed, deduplicated postings with real location granularity rather than a scraped string that says "Remote (EU) — or Stockholm". Frequently asked questions Do I need a Teamtailor API key? No. The jobs.json feed is public per career site. You supply company subdomains; we handle the fetching, pacing, and parsing. What happens if one of my companies doesn't exist? That subdomain is logged and skipped. Every other company in the same run still returns its rows — a typo in a 50-company list costs you one company, not the run. Why is description_html empty by default? It's opt-in via includeHtml . Raw markup is usually the biggest field in the dataset and most pipelines discard it, so we don't ship it unless you ask. Why is job_id sometimes null? Because the feed sent an identifier that isn't a valid integer. We keep the row and null the field rather than failing the item — job_url is always present and is a reliable unique key. title: 300 cities, 300 column names: normalizing Socrata building permits

title: '5 to 9 hours' has to become a number: normalizing Viator + GetYourGuide
author: Devil Scrapes
summary: Quick answer Viator and GetYourGuide list overlapping tour-and-activity inventory, but neither platform writes a duration or a price the same way the other does — "5 to 9 hours" on one card, "2.5 hours" on the next, a euro symbol here and a plain number there. title: Stack Exchange tells you exactly how long to wait — most scrapers ignore it
author: Devil Scrapes
summary: Quick answer The official Stack Overflow data dump has been paused since mid-2025, and even active it was a quarterly, multi-gigabyte XML export you had to ETL yourself before it was useful. The live Stack Exchange API ( api.stackexchange.com/2.3 ) is the fresher alternative, but it caps unauthenticated traffic at 300 requests/day and tells every client, on every page, exactly how many seconds to wait before the next request — a signal most naive scrapers ignore. Stack Exchange's API does something more precise — its JSON response body carries an optional backoff field, a number of seconds the server wants you to wait before your next request, sent proactively rather than as a punishment after you've already been throttled. The scraper reads that field on every page and sleeps for exactly what it says, plus a one-second guard margin, before issuing the next request — not a fixed delay, not an exponentially-doubling guess, but the number the API itself hands back. title: We scanned 671 MCP servers to see what happens when an agent retries
author: aurumflux20
summary: Every timeout is a question nobody can answer: did it happen? An agent calls a tool. The call times out. The agent doesn't know whether the email sent, the invoice was created, the charge went through. So it retries — because that's what agents do. If nothing on either side of that call can tell the second attempt from the first, the effect happens twice. We wanted to know how common that is in practice, so we scanned the ecosystem: 671 MCP servers, 27,153 declared tools. What we found Servers scanned successfully 671 (of 755 attempted) Tools declared across them 27,153 Servers performing real writes 539 (80%) Of those, with zero visible idempotency guards 175 (32%) Servers with retry logic and zero guards 40 Servers with money-adjacent tools and no visible guard 35 Servers with no guard of any kind, anywhere 288 (42%) The sharpest cut — servers that write, retry, and have no guard the scanner could see — is 32 servers with 28,653 combined monthly downloads. Those are the places where a timeout is most likely to become a duplicate. Among the 23 largest servers we scanned (10,000+ downloads/month), 6 perform writes with no visible guard. What this scan cannot see — read this before quoting the numbers This is the most important section, so it goes before the analysis rather than after. A scanner reading a repository from the outside usually cannot prove a double-fire. Three reasons, each of which we hit repeatedly: The guard often lives somewhere else. Many servers call a backend that deduplicates on its own — a payment API keyed by a nonce, a database with a unique constraint. From the client repo, that protection is invisible. "No guard found" means the scanner found none in this code , not "this software is unsafe." A tool that looks like a write may not be one. We found tools that appear to send payments but only return a link for a human to sign. Names lie in both directions. Our own scanner has been wrong. An early version accused a repo of having zero idempotency guards while it shipped an entire module of them — a regex with no word boundary couldn't match deriveIdempotencyKey . It hand-verified at 3 of 7 on its first real targets. Every pattern in the current version exists because an earlier one got something wrong. So these numbers describe what is visible in public code , not a safety verdict on any project. We're publishing aggregates and no names. If you want to know about a specific server, the honest answer is: read it, and ask the maintainer what the backend does. We also excluded failures rather than counting them as zeros: 66 repositories failed to clone, 17 returned unparseable output, 1 crashed the scanner. A failed lookup is not a finding. Including them would have made every percentage look worse and been wrong. Why the pattern shows up so consistently Idempotency isn't hard because the code is hard. A lease, a key, a stored result — that's an afternoon. It's hard because it asks a question most systems never make explicit: What makes two operations the same operation? Get that answer too narrow and you get false duplicates: annoying, safe, loud. Get it too wide and you get silent data loss — two legitimately different actions collapsing into one, where the second silently returns the first one's receipt. That failure looks like success. Nobody investigates a transaction that appears to have worked. We learned this the expensive way. We proposed an idempotency key to a payments project derived from URL, amount, and wallet. A stranger pointed out it omitted payee, network, and asset — meaning two genuinely different purchases would have collapsed into one. Our fix would have been worse than the bug. MCP makes this sharper than ordinary API design, for a structural reason: the caller is a language model. It doesn't know your retry semantics, it can't read your backend, and when a call fails ambiguously its instinct is to try again. In the servers we read, the tool schema is where that knowledge would have to live — and it's usually silent. What actually helps Three things, in order of effort: Say it in the schema. If a tool is unsafe to retry blindly, the description is the only place the model will read it. One sentence: "if this times out, the operation may have completed — check before retrying." Costs nothing, and it's the single highest-leverage change we've seen. Accept a caller-supplied key. Let the caller mark two attempts as the same attempt. Don't derive it from the payload alone. Make the choke point atomic. Whatever admits the effect should also be what checks whether it already happened. Check your own server npx fencescan Zero dependencies, no install, no account. It reports candidates and evidence, never verdicts, for the reasons above. If it flags something you know is guarded, that's a bug worth reporting to us — a false positive costs more than a miss. Methodology, the full pattern list, and the four failure modes we've fixed: https://github.com/aurumflux20/fencescan If you want to see the failure mode rather than read about it, here are 1,000 concurrent agents trying to charge the same card, with and without a guard: https://aurumflux20.github.io/once-kernel-ts/ We build open-source retry-safety tooling ( once-kernel , effectfence ), which is why we had a scanner pointed at this in the first place. The numbers are the numbers either way — and the caveats above are what keep them worth reading.

title: GitAscii vs github-readme-stats: Moving from Query Strings to Edge Rendering 🚀
author: Igor Braz
summary: The classic github-readme-stats has been the undisputed king of profile customization for years. We have all seen the familiar stats cards pinned to thousands of developer portfolios. But relying on query parameters appended directly to an image tag introduces structural bottlenecks when you want true creative freedom and optimal load performance. title: Building a Global eSIM Platform: Why I Chose This Stack Over Traditional SIM Cards
author: Wae Luxe
summary: The Problem: Why Physical SIM Cards Are Broken I've traveled to 30+ countries, and every single time, the same ritual: land at the airport, find a SIM card kiosk, show my passport, wait 20 minutes for activation, and pray the data actually works. It's 2026, and we're still doing this. Physical SIM cards are a relic of 1991 — a piece of plastic with a chip that locks you into one carrier, one country, one plan. If you're a digital nomad hopping between Thailand, Vietnam, and Indonesia, you're buying three different SIMs. If you're a business traveler doing London → Dubai → Singapore, you're either paying $10/day roaming fees or juggling SIM cards like a street magician. The numbers are staggering: the global travel SIM market is worth over $10 billion, and most of it runs on physical cards distributed through airport kiosks and convenience stores. The friction is real — and it's entirely unnecessary. So I decided to build iWanteSIM , a global eSIM platform that lets travelers buy data plans instantly, activate them in under 60 seconds, and stay connected across 200+ countries — without ever touching a physical SIM card. Here's the full story of the tech stack, the architecture decisions, and the carrier integration nightmares I didn't see coming. The Core Architecture: What Powers a Global eSIM Platform When I started architecting this, I knew the stack had to handle three things really well: Real-time eSIM provisioning — generating and delivering eSIM profiles to users' devices within seconds of purchase Multi-carrier orchestration — talking to dozens of mobile network operators (MNOs) across 200+ countries, each with their own API quirks Global coverage routing — intelligently selecting the best carrier profile based on the user's destination, device compatibility, and real-time network availability Here's the stack I landed on after months of prototyping: Backend: Node.js + PostgreSQL + Redis I chose Node.js for the API layer because eSIM provisioning is inherently I/O-bound. You're making API calls to carrier partners, waiting for SM-DP+ (Subscription Manager Data Preparation) servers to generate profiles, and handling webhooks for activation status. Node's event loop is perfect for this — non-blocking I/O means one server can handle thousands of concurrent provisioning requests without breaking a sweat. PostgreSQL handles the relational data: user accounts, orders, eSIM profiles (ICCID, activation codes, QR payloads), carrier contracts, and pricing tables. The schema is normalized but denormalized where it matters — the esim_profiles table is the hot path, queried on every purchase and activation. Redis is the secret sauce. eSIM profile generation takes 2-8 seconds depending on the carrier, so I pre-generate and cache profiles in Redis. When a user buys a plan for Thailand, we pop a pre-provisioned profile from the queue, assign it to their order, and deliver the QR code instantly. No waiting. The cache also holds rate-limit counters for carrier APIs (some MNOs cap you at 100 requests/minute), session tokens, and real-time activation status. Frontend: Next.js + Tailwind The customer-facing side is Next.js with server-side rendering for SEO (critical for an e-commerce platform). The checkout flow is a single-page experience: select country → pick plan → pay → get QR code. Tailwind keeps the UI clean and responsive — most users are on mobile, often on spotty airport Wi-Fi, so the bundle has to be lean. The QR code rendering uses qrcode (82M monthly npm downloads) with error correction level H (30% recovery) — because if a traveler's screen is cracked or dim, that QR still needs to scan. The Hard Part: Carrier Integrations This is where things got real. Integrating with mobile carriers is nothing like integrating with Stripe or Twilio. The telecom industry runs on protocols designed in the 1990s — GSMA specifications like SGP.22 (consumer eSIM) and SGP.32 (IoT eSIM) are dense, 300-page documents written by committee. I evaluated three approaches: Option 1: Direct MNO Integration Sign individual contracts with every carrier in every country. This gives you the best margins but requires legal teams, local entities, and months of negotiation per carrier. For 200+ countries, this is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar undertaking. Hard pass for a startup. Option 2: eSIM Aggregators (Gigs, 1Global, Celitech) These companies act as middlemen — they've already done the carrier deals and expose a unified API. You call one endpoint to provision an eSIM for any supported country, and they handle the carrier-specific complexity behind the scenes. Gigs — Great API design, developer-first documentation, supports smartphones and wearables. Their API lets you create subscriptions, manage plans, and handle porting. Pricing is transparent but margins are thinner since they take a cut. 1Global — Massive coverage (190+ countries, 600+ networks), runs their own core network infrastructure. They're more enterprise-focused with IoT/M2M support and compliance features (MiFID recording for financial services). Celitech — Built specifically for travel providers (OTAs, airlines, hotels). SOC 2 certified, US-hosted, and designed for embedding eSIM sales into existing booking flows. Their API is literally "one line of code" for basic integration. Option 3: Hybrid — What I Actually Built I went with a hybrid model. For the MVP, I integrated with two eSIM aggregators as primary providers, giving me instant coverage across 200+ countries without signing a single carrier contract. The aggregator API abstracts away the GSMA protocol complexity — I don't need to understand SM-DP+ server addressing or profile type coding. But here's the key architectural decision: I built an abstraction layer between my platform and the aggregators. Every carrier partner (aggregator or direct MNO) implements a common interface: interface ESimProvider { getCoverage (): Promise < Country [] > ; getPlans ( country : string ): Promise < Plan [] > ; provisionProfile ( plan : Plan , user : User ): Promise < EsimProfile > ; getActivationStatus ( iccid : string ): Promise < ActivationStatus > ; getUsage ( iccid : string ): Promise < DataUsage > ; } This means I can swap aggregators, add direct carrier relationships, or A/B test providers without touching the rest of the platform. Today I'm using aggregators for speed; tomorrow I can negotiate direct MNO deals for better margins and plug them in through the same interface. The lesson: never couple your business logic to a third-party API . Telecom APIs change, carriers get acquired, aggregators raise prices. The abstraction layer is cheap to build upfront and priceless when you need to pivot. Real-Time Provisioning: The 60-Second Challenge My goal was simple: from "I want an eSIM" to "I'm connected" in under 60 seconds. Here's what actually happens behind the scenes when a user buys a plan: Order received (0-100ms) — API validates the order, checks inventory, reserves a pre-cached eSIM profile from Redis Payment processed (100-500ms) — Stripe handles the payment; webhook confirms success Profile provisioning (500ms-8s) — API calls the aggregator to activate the eSIM profile for the user's device. This is the bottleneck — some carriers are fast (2s), others take 8s because their SM-DP+ servers are, frankly, ancient QR code delivery (immediate) — User receives a QR code (LPA-compliant) via email and on-screen. Scanning it triggers the eSIM download on their device Activation confirmation (5-30s after scan) — Webhook from the carrier confirms the profile is active. User is online. The pre-caching strategy in Redis was the breakthrough. Without it, every purchase would trigger a synchronous provisioning call that takes 2-8 seconds — unacceptable for a checkout flow. With pre-caching, the user waits only for payment processing, and provisioning happens asynchronously. By the time they finish reading the "How to install your eSIM" instructions, the profile is ready. API Design Decisions I'd Make Again 1. Idempotency Keys on Every Mutation When you're dealing with carrier APIs that sometimes timeout without confirming whether a profile was created, idempotency is non-negotiable. Every order creation, profile provisioning, and activation request carries an idempotency key. If a request fails and retries, the carrier recognizes the key and returns the original result instead of creating a duplicate profile (and charging me twice). 2. Webhook-First Architecture Carrier activation status doesn't change on a predictable schedule. Polling every 30 seconds wastes API quota and adds latency. Instead, the platform exposes webhook endpoints that carriers call when a profile activates, deactivates, or hits a data threshold. The internal event bus (Redis pub/sub) fans out these events to update user dashboards, send email notifications, and trigger usage alerts. 3. Graceful Degradation If a carrier's API is down (it happens more often than you'd think), the platform doesn't fail. It falls back to a secondary provider for that country, or queues the order for retry with exponential backoff. Users see "Your eSIM is being prepared — we'll notify you when it's ready" instead of an error page. This alone reduced support tickets by 40%. What I Got Wrong (And Fixed) No building-in-public story is complete without the failures: Mistake #1: Underestimating carrier API inconsistency. I assumed RESTful APIs with consistent JSON responses. Reality: one carrier returns activation status as "ACTIVE" , another returns 1 , a third returns {"state": "activated", "timestamp": ...} . I now run every carrier response through a normalization layer that maps all variants to a canonical format. This is tedious but essential. Mistake #2: Not planning for eSIM profile exhaustion. Each eSIM profile (ICCID) is a finite resource. Aggregators allocate a pool of profiles per partner, and when you run out, provisioning fails silently. I learned this the hard way during a traffic spike from a travel blog feature — 200 orders failed because the profile pool was empty. Now there's a monitoring dashboard with alerts at 20% and 50% pool depletion, plus automatic top-up requests to the aggregator. Mistake #3: QR code rendering on low-end devices. The first version used a canvas-based QR renderer that broke on older Android phones common in Southeast Asian markets. Switched to server-side QR generation with SVG fallback. Works everywhere now. Why This Stack Over Traditional SIM Cards? The traditional SIM card supply chain looks like this: manufacturer → distributor → retailer → customer. Each step adds cost, delay, and plastic waste. An eSIM platform collapses that into: API → device. No manufacturing, no shipping, no inventory, no landfill. For the business, the unit economics are transformative. A physical SIM costs $0.50-2.00 to manufacture, package, and distribute. An eSIM profile costs fractions of a cent to generate. The margin difference alone makes the platform viable at scale. For users, the experience is night and day. Instead of hunting for a SIM card shop in a foreign airport at 2 AM, they buy a plan on their phone before takeoff and activate it the moment they land. If you want to understand how eSIM activation actually works, I wrote a detailed guide on setting up your first eSIM that walks through the process step by step. And if you're still wondering what an eSIM even is, here's a clear explanation: What is an eSIM and how does it work? What's Next The platform is live and processing orders across 200+ countries, but there's a long roadmap ahead: Direct carrier partnerships — Moving from 100% aggregator-dependent to a mix of direct MNO relationships for better margins on high-volume routes (Europe, Southeast Asia, North America) IoT/M2M support — eSIM isn't just for phones. Connected cars, smart meters, and asset trackers all need cellular connectivity, and the SGP.32 standard makes IoT eSIM provisioning viable Usage-based pricing — Most eSIM plans today are fixed-duration (7 days, 30 days). Pay-as-you-go data, like AWS for connectivity, is the endgame Open-source the abstraction layer — The provider interface I built could help other developers integrate with eSIM aggregators without reinventing the wheel The Bottom Line Building an eSIM platform is 20% standard web development and 80% telecom industry wrangling. The tech stack (Node.js, PostgreSQL, Redis, Next.js) is straightforward — any competent full-stack developer could build the scaffolding in a week. The hard part is navigating carrier relationships, understanding GSMA specifications, and building resilience against API failures that are outside your control. But the opportunity is massive. Physical SIM cards are going the way of the floppy disk, and someone is going to build the Stripe for global connectivity. I'm betting it can be us. What's your experience with eSIM? Have you built anything in the telecom space, or are you still juggling physical SIMs when you travel? I'd love to hear your war stories in the comments.

title: ShowDev: I built a bulk HTML-to-Markdown converter that runs entirely in the browser
author: Christoph Dieck
summary: Most HTML-to-Markdown tools handle one file at a time. You paste some HTML, get Markdown back, repeat. That works for a quick snippet but not when you have 200+ pages from a help center export sitting in a folder. I needed exactly that. I had a full site mirror (grabbed with wget --mirror ) and wanted clean Markdown I could feed into an LLM knowledge base. Nothing I found could handle it without uploading files to a server or converting one by one. So I built HTML to Markdown AI . How it works You drop a ZIP file (or individual HTML files) into the browser A Go-based conversion pipeline compiled to WebAssembly processes everything locally You get a ZIP back with clean GitHub-Flavored Markdown, folder structure preserved No server involved. Your files never leave your machine. The conversion pipeline The heavy lifting happens in Go/WASM. The pipeline: Strips navigation, footers, scripts, styles, and other boilerplate noise Extracts the main content from the page Converts to GFM with proper heading hierarchy, tables, code blocks, and links Handles batch processing so you can throw hundreds of files at it Why no built-in crawler? Intentional decision. Downloading HTML from someone else's site has legal implications depending on jurisdiction and terms of service. I don't want to be in that business. Downloading is also the easy part: wget -r -l 0 -np -k -E -p -e robots = off \ --reject-regex '\.(png|jpe?g|gif|svg|webp|woff2?|ttf|css|js|zip|pdf)$' \ -w 0.5 --random-wait \ https://docs.example.com/ That gives you a local folder with all the HTML. The hard and annoying part is turning that into clean, usable Markdown. That's what this tool solves. Stack Frontend: Astro + Tailwind Conversion engine: Go compiled to WebAssembly Processing: Entirely client-side, zero backend Try it https://www.html-to-markdown-ai.com Use cases I've tested it with: Help center exports (Zendesk, Confluence, custom wikis) Documentation sites mirrored with wget/httrack Scraped content for RAG pipelines Training data prep for fine-tuning If you work with LLMs and regularly need to get web content into a format they can digest, this might save you some time. title: OOP Object-Oriented Programming
author: Mohamed Fakhr
summary: Advantages of using OOP: Is faster and easier to execute. Provides a clear structure for the programs. Helps to keep code DRY "Don't Repeat Yourself" and makes code easier to maintain, modify, and debug. Makes it possible to create fully reusable applications with less code and shorter development time. Define a Class: A class is defined by using the class keyword, followed by the name of the class and a pair of curly braces {} . All its properties and methods go inside the braces. Delegation: Delegation means that you use an object of another class as an instance variable. We can create multiple objects from a class. Each object has all the variables and functions defined in the class. An object of a class is made using the new keyword. Note: The $this keyword refers to the current class and is only available inside methods. __construct() function: Automatically runs at the beginning of the class. __destruct() function: Automatically runs at the end of the class. Encapsulation: The wrapping up of data and methods is a protection mechanism for the variables and functions inside the class. Access Modifier: Public: Variables or functions can be accessed from everywhere. Private: Variables or functions can ONLY be accessed inside the class. Protected: Variables or functions can be accessed inside the class and by child classes that extend from the parent class. Constants: It can’t be changed once it is declared. Declared inside a class with the const keyword. It is recommended to name the constants in all uppercase letters . Access outside the class by using the class name followed by the scope resolution operator :: . Access a constant inside the class by using the self keyword. Static Functions and Variables: Static functions or variables can be called directly - without creating an instance of the class first. Static functions or variables are declared with the static keyword. To access a static function or variable, use the class name , double colon :: , and the function name . A static function can be accessed from a function in the same class using the self keyword and double colon :: . To call a static method from a child class, use the parent keyword inside the child class. The static method can be public or protected. Note: The final keyword can be used to prevent class inheritance or to prevent method overriding. Polymorphism: is one of the OOP features that allows us to perform a single action in different ways. Like declaring a function in the parent class and giving the function a different implementation in the children's classes. Abstract: Can have both abstract methods (without body) and regular methods (with implementation). Can have properties (variables). A class can extended single abstract (single inheritance). Cannot be instantiated directly — only extended (inherited) by other classes. Used when classes share some common behavior, but also need to implement some parts individually. Interface: Can only contain method declarations (no implementation). No properties — only method signatures. A class can implement multiple interfaces (multiple inheritance). Forces the class to implement all methods defined in the interface. Traits PHP only supports single inheritance: a child class can inherit from only one parent. So, what if a class needs to inherit multiple behaviors? OOP traits solve this problem. Traits are used to declare functions that can be used in multiple classes. Traits can have functions and abstract functions that can be used in multiple classes, and the functions can have any access modifier (public, private, or protected). Traits are declared with the trait keyword. To use a trait in a class, use the use keyword. Difference between Traits and Interfaces in PHP many classes implement the same interface but have different behavior, while traits are just chunks of code injected into a class in PHP.

title: When an AI Tool Shuts Down: How to Avoid Lock-in and Keep Your Data
author: AI Video Generator Free
summary: When an AI Tool Shuts Down: How to Avoid Lock-in and Keep Your Data AI tools disappear more often than people expect. A startup pivots, a feature moves behind a paywall, or a service goes offline with short notice. This guide covers how to read an AI tool's staying power before you depend on it, and how to keep your work portable so a shutdown does not erase weeks of effort. Why AI tools disappear New AI products launch every week, and many close just as fast. A team runs out of funding, gets acquired and then shelved, or rebrands into something unrelated. When your workflow depends on one tool, that risk becomes your problem. Treating any single AI service as permanent is the main mistake to avoid. Read the signals before you commit Before you build on a tool, check a few basics. Is there a published export option or an API? Does the company post updates and something resembling a roadmap? Is there a real paying customer base, or is everything free with no clear revenue model? Free with no revenue is a yellow flag for how long the service will last. If you want to compare options side by side before picking, an AI tools directory lets you scan categories and features in one place instead of juggling a dozen bookmarks. Keep your source files The simplest hedge is to never let the tool be the only place your work lives. Save the original prompts, the input files, and the output to your own storage. If a tool generates images, keep the prompts and seed values. If it writes copy, keep the drafts as plain text. This habit takes a few seconds per task and saves hours of reconstruction later. Prefer tools with an API and export A tool that exposes an API or a clean export gives you an exit. You can pull your data out on a schedule and back it up yourself. Tools that only let you view results inside their app, with no export button, carry the most risk. Before you invest time in learning one, confirm that you can leave with your data in hand. Have a fallback for core tasks For any task that matters, know one or two alternatives. If your image generator stops working tomorrow, you should be able to switch within a day rather than spend a week relearning from scratch. Writing down the prompt templates that worked means the next tool can reuse them with small edits. What to do the day a tool announces closure If a tool posts a shutdown notice, act fast but in order. First, export everything, including account settings and saved presets, because that data often goes first. Second, note which tasks the tool handled and line up a replacement before the deadline. Third, test the replacement on one real project before you migrate everything, so you catch gaps early instead of mid-deadline. Frequently asked questions How much warning do you usually get before an AI tool shuts down? It varies a lot. Some give weeks of notice and an export window. Others go offline with a short blog post. Assume the short-notice case and export on a regular schedule. Is an open-source model safer than a hosted tool? Running your own model removes the shutdown risk, but it adds setup and hardware cost. For most people, a hosted tool with a solid export is a reasonable middle ground. What should I back up first? Start with anything you cannot recreate easily: finished work, custom prompts, and any saved settings or presets. Plan for the exit from day one The tools that hurt most when they disappear are the ones you never planned to leave. Pick tools you can leave, keep your data in your own hands, and write down what worked. A shutdown then becomes an annoyance rather than a crisis. summary: The Rise of Agentic AI: Understanding AI Agents, Their Definition, and Future Impact Artificial intelligence continues its rapid evolution, introducing groundbreaking paradigms that redefine our interaction with technology. To truly grasp the significance of this technological leap, we must first answer the fundamental question: what is agentic AI ? In its simplest form, agentic AI refers to intelligent systems that can operate with a high degree of autonomy, making decisions and taking actions without constant human intervention. Unlike traditional AI models that might perform a single, predefined task, agentic AI systems are designed to perceive their environment, reason about their observations, plan a sequence of actions, and execute those actions to achieve a specific objective. They are goal-oriented, often iterative, and capable of self-correction. Imagine an AI that doesn't just write code when prompted, but understands a complex software requirement, breaks it down into smaller tasks, writes the code, tests it, identifies bugs, and then iteratively refines the solution until the initial requirement is met. This is the essence of agentic AI . Agentic AI Definition: Delving Deeper A more formal agentic AI definition highlights its key attributes: autonomy, proactivity, social ability (in some cases), and reactivity. An AI agent is a software entity that is situated in an environment, and can act autonomously in that environment to achieve goals. It's not just about reacting to inputs, but initiating actions based on an internal model of the world and a set of predefined objectives. This capability allows AI agents to engage in complex problem-solving, learn from experiences, and adapt their behavior over time. For businesses, understanding what is an AI agent is crucial. These agents can automate multi-step processes, manage complex workflows, and even engage in strategic decision-making, significantly boosting efficiency and innovation. The ability of an AI agent to operate independently, continuously optimizing its approach, makes it a powerful tool for modern enterprises. The Core Principles of AI Agents At the heart of AI agents lies a set of foundational principles that differentiate them from other AI forms: Goal-Oriented Behavior : Every AI agent has a defined objective. Its actions are geared towards achieving this goal, even if it requires multiple steps and iterations. Perception : Agents must be able to sense or receive information from their environment, whether it's digital data, sensor inputs, or user commands. Reasoning and Planning : Based on perceived information and its goals, an AI agent can reason about the best course of action and formulate a plan. Action : Agents execute their plans, interacting with their environment to bring about desired changes. Memory and Learning : Advanced AI agents can remember past states and actions, learning from successes and failures to improve future performance. Generative AI, exemplified by large language models (LLMs) like GPT, excels at creating novel content – text, images, code, or audio – based on prompts. Its primary function is generation. An AI agent , however, might use generative AI as a tool within its broader operational framework. For example, an AI agent tasked with building a website might use a generative AI model to create content or generate initial code snippets. But the agent itself is responsible for the entire process: understanding the request, breaking it down, using tools (including generative AI), executing steps, testing, and iterating until the website is complete. The distinction in generative AI vs agentic AI lies in the scope of their operation: generative AI focuses on creation, while agentic AI focuses on autonomous action and goal achievement, often orchestrating multiple tools and models. title: I have 591 pages. Google indexed one. Here's how I'm debugging it.
author: Bcrypto
summary: I run a directory site with 2,499 real vendor listings across Beirut, Dubai, Riyadh, Doha, Cairo and Casablanca. It has 591 programmatic landing pages and 1,182 URLs in its sitemap. I checked what Google had actually indexed. The homepage. That was it. Not 591. Not 200. One. This post is what I checked, what I ruled out, and the one diagnostic that actually decides what to do about it — because I got that last part wrong at first, and I suspect a lot of people do. First instinct: something's broken on the site That's where I went, and it's usually where everyone goes. So I worked the checklist. robots.txt — correct. Allows everything, references the sitemap. Sitemap — valid XML, 1,182 URLs, auto-generated, submitted. Hub page — present. Something links into the page set; they aren't orphans. Internal linking — 62 cross-links per page. Not a dead end. Structured data — JSON-LD on every page. Server-rendered content — real listings in the initial HTML. Not a JS shell. Here's the fastest way to check that last one, and it's the one people skip: curl -s https://yoursite.com/some-page | wc -w If that number is small, that's roughly what a crawler sees. Your framework hydrating beautifully in a browser is irrelevant to a bot that doesn't run JavaScript. I've measured client sites with 10 words in the initial HTML that looked perfect to a human. All six checks passed. Which meant the problem wasn't on the page. The wrong conclusion I nearly published My first explanation was: the site has no inbound links and no brand mentions anywhere, so Google has no reason to crawl it deeply. Authority problem. Go get links. That's a coherent story. It might even be right. But I nearly wrote it up as fact, and it turns out there's a specific piece of data that decides it — and until you look at that data, you're guessing. The diagnostic that actually matters Google Search Console → Indexing → Pages → "Why pages aren't indexed". Two statuses look similar and mean opposite things: Discovered – currently not indexed Google knows the URL exists but hasn't spent crawl budget on it. This is the authority/crawl-scheduling case. Links and internal-linking improvements genuinely help here. Crawled – currently not indexed Google fetched the page, looked at it, and decided not to index it. This is a quality judgement . For programmatic pages — city × category templates where only a couple of fields change — this usually means it read them as thin or near-duplicate. If it's the second one, backlinks will not fix it. You can build links for six months and stay at one indexed page, because the pages themselves are what got rejected. The fix is consolidation: fewer, substantially different pages with real unique content, rather than more thin ones. Same symptom. Opposite remedies. The export is free and takes two minutes, and I was about to skip it in favour of a narrative that felt right. The trap in programmatic SEO Programmatic SEO makes the satisfying work and the useful work feel identical. Generating 600 pages is a fun afternoon. It produces a number that goes up. It looks like progress. And if your pages are being rejected rather than not reached , generating another 600 moves you from one indexed page to one indexed page. I could have shipped a second batch and felt productive the whole time. What I'd check on any site, in order site:yourdomain.com in Google. Compare the count to how many pages you think you have. The gap is the actual story, and most people never look. View source with JS disabled. If there's a loading spinner where your content should be, that's what you've published. GSC → Indexing → Pages. Get the real status before choosing a fix. Check whether you're blocking AI crawlers. Plenty of robots.txt files disallow GPTBot , ClaudeBot or PerplexityBot inherited from a template, and then people wonder why assistants never cite them: curl -s https://yoursite.com/robots.txt | grep -iE "gptbot|claudebot|perplexity" Grep your bundles for keys. Unrelated to indexing, but while you're in there — anything starting sk_live , AKIA , or a service-role JWT that reached the browser is public regardless of what your backend does. Where I've got to The GSC export is the next thing I do, and it decides whether the next month is spent earning citations or consolidating pages. I'm writing this before I have that answer deliberately, because the interesting part isn't the resolution — it's that the symptom looked obvious and pointed at two incompatible fixes. If you've got a programmatic site sitting at a fraction of its expected index coverage, check which status you have before you spend a month on the wrong one. I automated the on-page half of these checks into a free scanner while debugging this — preflightscan.vercel.app , no signup. It won't tell you your GSC status; nothing can except GSC.
